section.title: Peter's Deliverance and the Death of Herod
section.sectionRationale: The gospel has just leapt to the Gentiles at Antioch, and now the church in Jerusalem meets a fresh wave of state persecution. Herod kills James and seizes Peter, but the praying church watches God break iron chains open and, soon after, strike down the proud king. The chapter is a study in two thrones: the earthly king who takes glory to himself and is eaten by worms, and the heavenly King whose word cannot be chained.
section.thesis: A king may kill an apostle and imprison another, but the ascended Christ hears His praying church, rescues His servant, judges the ruler who steals God's glory, and keeps His word spreading and multiplying no matter who opposes it.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: James killed and Peter imprisoned while the church prays; the night rescue by the angel; the joyful confusion at Mary's house; and the death of Herod, closing with the word of God still advancing.

units.label: James killed, Peter imprisoned
units.note: the sword falls, but the church prays

verses.text: About that time, King Herod reached out to harm some who belonged to the church.
He had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword.
And seeing that this pleased the Jews, Herod proceeded to seize Peter during the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
He arrested him and put him in prison, handing him over to be guarded by four squads of four soldiers each. Herod intended to bring him out to the people after the Passover.
So Peter was kept in prison, but the {{ekklesia|church}} was fervently praying to God for him.

units.label: The angel and the open gate
units.note: chains fall off, iron gates open by themselves

verses.text: On the night before Herod was to bring him to trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, with sentries standing guard at the entrance to the prison.
Suddenly an {{angelos|angel}} of the Lord appeared and a light shone in the cell. He tapped Peter on the side and woke him up, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his wrists.
“Get dressed and put on your sandals,” said the angel. Peter did so, and the angel told him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.”
So Peter followed him out, but he was unaware that what the angel was doing was real. He thought he was only seeing a vision.

They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate leading to the city, which opened for them by itself. When they had gone outside and walked the length of one block, the angel suddenly left him.
Then Peter came to himself and said, “Now I know for sure that the Lord has sent His angel and rescued me from Herod’s grasp and from everything the Jewish people were anticipating.”

units.label: The knock at Mary's gate
units.note: the praying church can hardly believe its own prayer

verses.text: And when he had realized this, he went to the house of Mary the mother of John, also called Mark, where many people had gathered together and were praying.
He knocked at the outer gate, and a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer it.
When she recognized Peter’s voice, she was so overjoyed that she forgot to open the gate, but ran inside and announced, “Peter is standing at the gate!”
“You are out of your mind,” they told her. But when she kept insisting it was so, they said, “It must be his angel.”
But Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened the door and saw him, they were astounded.
Peter motioned with his hand for silence, and he described how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. “Send word to James and to the brothers,” he said, and he left for another place.

units.label: The death of Herod
units.note: the king who took God's glory is struck down

verses.text: At daybreak there was no small commotion among the soldiers as to what had become of Peter.
After Herod had searched for him unsuccessfully, he examined the guards and ordered that they be executed. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent some time there.

Now Herod was in a furious dispute with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they convened before him. Having secured the support of Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their region depended on the king’s country for food.
On the appointed day, Herod donned his royal robes, sat on his throne, and addressed the people.
And they began to shout, “This is the voice of a god, not a man!”
Immediately, because Herod did not give glory to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died.

units.label: The word keeps spreading
units.note: the true King's word cannot be chained

verses.text: But the {{logos|word}} of God continued to spread and multiply.
When Barnabas and Saul had fulfilled their mission to Jerusalem, they returned, bringing with them John, also called Mark.

ekklesia.gloss: The assembly, the called-out people of God. Luke sets the praying ekklesia over against the armed power of Herod. The church has no sword and no political leverage, only prayer, yet it is the church, not the king, that prevails.

angelos.gloss: A messenger, an angel. The same word carries two errands in this chapter: an angel of the Lord frees Peter and, in verse 23, an angel of the Lord strikes Herod. The unseen court of heaven serves the ascended Christ, rescuing His servant and judging His rival.

logos.gloss: Word, message. The logos of God is the true subject of Acts. Kings die and apostles are jailed, but the word of God spreads and multiplies, growing like a living thing that no prison and no throne can contain.

basic.context: The church at Antioch has just been born and the gospel is reaching Gentiles. Back in Jerusalem, King Herod Agrippa launches a persecution to win favour with his people. He kills the apostle James and arrests Peter, planning a public execution after Passover. The church cannot fight back, so it does the one thing it can: it gathers and prays through the night. God answers by sending an angel who walks Peter straight out of a maximum-security prison, and not long after strikes down the king who lets the crowd hail him as a god.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the chapter as a deliberate contrast between two rulers. Herod grasps at glory and ends eaten by worms; the ascended Christ quietly rescues His servant and keeps His word advancing. Notice that God did not spare James but did rescue Peter, so the point is not that the faithful never suffer, but that God reigns over life, death, prison, and thrones. The last verse is the punchline: the word of God continued to spread and multiply.
basic.originalLanguages: Three words carry the chapter. The praying ekklesia, the church, is set against the king's soldiers. The angelos, the angel of the Lord, both frees Peter and later strikes Herod, showing heaven's court at work. And the logos, the word of God, is the true hero: it keeps spreading and multiplying while a king lies dead.
basic.typology: Peter's rescue echoes the exodus: it happens at Passover, chains fall, gates open, and God leads His servant out by night, just as He led Israel out of Egypt. The pattern points to the greater rescue Christ works, leading His people out of the prison of sin and death.
basic.christ: Peter walks free, but the pattern points beyond him. Where Peter was delivered from death, Christ went through death and out the other side, His tomb opened not by an angel unlocking a gate but by resurrection power. The ascended Christ is the true King whose word cannot be chained, in contrast to Herod who steals glory and dies.
basic.god: God is sovereign over kings and prisons. He is not absent when James dies, nor overpowered when Peter is chained. He hears the prayers of a powerless church, sends His angel, and will not share His glory with a preening king. He is both the rescuer of His servants and the judge of the proud.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 2 shows the nations raging while God installs His King. Daniel 4 shows a proud king humbled for refusing to honour God. Exodus 12 gives the Passover backdrop of Peter's night rescue. Isaiah 42:8 declares that God will not give His glory to another, the very sin that felled Herod.
basic.oneStory: This chapter belongs to the great movement of Acts: the ascended Christ pours out His Spirit and drives His gospel from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. Persecution and the death of an apostle cannot stop it, and neither can a king who thinks himself a god. The word of God keeps spreading, and Barnabas and Saul return with Mark, ready for the mission that fills the next chapters.

context.literary:
Luke builds the chapter in six panels that move like a short play. Verses 1 to 5 set the stage: a king, a dead apostle, an imprisoned one, and a praying church. Verses 6 to 11 are the escape, told in slow motion, with commands from the angel in quick succession, get up, dress, put on sandals, wrap your cloak, follow. Verses 12 to 17 are the comedy at the door, in which the rescued man is the one left standing outside. Verses 18 and 19 are a brief scene of the soldiers' fear and the guards' execution. Verses 20 to 23 are the king's end, and verses 24 and 25 are the summary that tells us which side won.

The symmetry is deliberate. The opening scene ends with a king planning an execution, and the closing scene with a king dying. The king who held a man in chains is struck by an angel, and the angel who opened the iron gate for Peter is the same kind of messenger who in verse 23 ends the king's life. Herod's soldiers search for Peter and cannot find him, verse 19, while the church that thought him lost finds him at the door. The chapter is a chain of reversals, and its centre is the quiet sentence of verse 5: Peter was kept in prison, but the church was fervently praying to God for him.

Luke also writes with humour. Peter is so deeply asleep that the angel has to strike his side. He thinks he is dreaming, verse 9. The servant girl Rhoda is so overjoyed that she leaves him standing outside. The praying church tells her she is out of her mind. The people who have prayed all night cannot believe the answer has come, and Luke does not hide it. The comedy is not mockery. It makes the divine action stand out against human slowness.

The chapter is also set between two visits to Jerusalem by Barnabas and Saul. The famine relief of 11:30 arrives, and in 12:25 they leave with John Mark, the same young man whose mother's house had been the place of prayer.
context.historical:
Herod Agrippa I was a grandson of Herod the Great and of the Hasmonean line through his grandmother Mariamne, which gave him a claim on Jewish loyalty that his relatives lacked. He grew up in Rome, was favoured by the emperors Caligula and Claudius, and was given the whole kingdom of his grandfather by AD 41. Josephus presents him as eager to appear pious in Jerusalem, and Luke's remark that he saw it pleased the Jews, verse 3, fits that picture: his rule depended on keeping the religious leadership content. This is the third Herod in the New Testament story, after Herod the Great who killed the infants, Matthew 2:16, and Antipas who mocked Jesus, Luke 23:11. His son Agrippa II will hear Paul's defence in Acts 26.

The arrest happens in the days of Unleavened Bread, and Herod plans a public trial after the Passover. The delay may reflect respect for the feast, since executing someone in the middle of the festival would be disruptive. The guard of four squads of four soldiers matches the Roman practice of watching in four night watches, each handled by a squad of four. Peter, chained to two soldiers with others at the door, was about as secure as a prisoner could be. The 'iron gate leading to the city' is part of the prison complex, whose exact location Luke does not say.

The church meets in the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark. The house has an outer gate and a servant, which suggests a family of some means. The 'James' of verse 17 is the Lord's brother, who by this time already had a prominent place, Galatians 1:19, and will preside at the council, Acts 15:13. Peter's departure to another place, verse 17, leaves Jerusalem's leadership to him.

Herod's death takes place at Caesarea in AD 44. Josephus records that at a festival Herod appeared in a robe woven with silver which shone in the morning sun, that his flatterers hailed him as a god, and that he was seized with violent stomach pains and died after five days. The accounts differ in detail but agree on the main points: public acclaim, a claim to divinity, sudden illness, and death. Tyre and Sidon depended on the king's territory for food, verse 20, an old arrangement going back to Solomon's wheat and oil for Hiram, 1 Kings 5:11, and relevant to the famine of 11:28.
context.canonical:
The chapter is an echo chamber. The first echo is the exodus. The timing at Passover, the angel's command to dress with sandals and cloak and to follow, and the unlocked gates all recall the instruction to eat the Passover fully dressed for travel, with sandals on the feet, Exodus 12:11, and the night when God struck down Egypt's firstborn and rescued Israel. A king who tried to hold God's people is judged, and the people are led out.

The second echo is Acts itself. In Acts 5:19 and 20 an angel had opened the doors of the jail and told the apostles to go and speak in the temple; there they went back to preach, and the Sanhedrin were left puzzled. Chapter 12 matches that scene in miracle but not in outcome, since Peter leaves for another place and James has already been killed. Luke is letting readers see that deliverance does not follow a template. The prayer of Acts 4:24 to 30, in which the church quoted Psalm 2 and recalled that Herod and Pilate had gathered against Jesus, finds its answer here in a later Herod's downfall.

The third echo is Daniel and Ezekiel. Nebuchadnezzar, in Daniel 4:30 to 31, was struck while the word of pride was still in his mouth, and Ezekiel told the ruler of Tyre that he had said 'I am a god' though he was a man and not a god, Ezekiel 28:2. Herod, whose audience came from Tyre and Sidon, has the same fate as the proud king of Tyre.

The fourth echo is in verse 24. 'The word of God continued to spread and multiply' recalls Genesis 1:28 and Exodus 1:7, where the Israelites were fruitful and multiplied under oppression. The same phrase had appeared in Acts 6:7 and will return in 19:20, forming a refrain through the book. Finally, Jesus had told James and John that they would drink His cup, Mark 10:39. James is the first of the Twelve to do so, verse 2, and Peter's own end is foretold in John 21:18 to 19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wrote for a church that still buried its martyrs and still lost its leaders. He does not tell the story of a rescue to make suffering seem unreal. He says in one clause that James was killed by the sword, and does not explain it. What he does explain, at length, is how God's people prevailed. They prayed, though without much expectation, and God acted in ways that made even the praying people gasp. He wanted them to learn that the church's weapons are not swords but prayer, and that their security does not lie in the survival of leaders.

The passage is also meant to unmask the pretensions of power. Herod sits on a throne in splendid robes and listens as a crowd calls him a god. Luke gives him no dialogue and no defence, only the verdict. A man who kills an apostle to please a crowd is himself killed for pleasing a crowd. Readers who live under rulers who claim too much are being told that God is never intimidated by thrones.

Luke closes with the line he cares about most. The king dies, and the word of God spreads. He wants the reader to leave not with Peter or Herod, but with the unstoppable word, and to see that the cause rests on God's hand and not on any single life.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Luke describes events without telling us what to make of them in rules. Herod's persecution, James's execution, Peter's escape, the prayer meeting and the king's death are all reported, and none is turned into a command. The point is not that every believer in prison should expect an angel, nor that every tyrant will be struck down in a public ceremony. History shows many faithful believers who died in prison and many cruel rulers who died in their beds.

What can be carried forward is what the narrative commends. The church prayed fervently and persistently, and Luke approves. Peter slept in peace on the night before his trial, which models trust, though Luke does not say it should be imitated by anyone who cannot. The household sharing the news shows hospitality in danger. The statement that Herod did not give glory to God states a principle that holds across the Bible, that those who take what belongs to God are in danger. The details of the escape, the angel's tap and the self-opening gate, are not a pattern for action, but they do teach that God can act when no human help is possible.

Take care also with the surprised prayer meeting. It is not a rule that prayer must lack faith to be answered, nor that it must be strong to be heard. Luke simply shows that God answers even weak and astonished prayer.

debates.question: Why did God rescue Peter but let James be killed?

views.label: Hidden sovereign purpose
views.case: Scripture gives no reason, and the strongest case is to rest in God's wisdom: He appointed Peter for further work and received James as a martyr, and both outcomes served the advance of the gospel. James's death is stated as plainly as Peter's rescue, so Luke will not let us treat deliverance as a formula.

views.label: The church's fervent prayer
views.case: Some point to the church praying earnestly for Peter, verse 5, as the difference. There is real weight here, for Luke deliberately notes the prayer, yet this must not become a rule that enough prayer always secures rescue, since faithful prayer does not always spare the martyr.

debates.bearing: Held rightly, the passage drives us to pray in faith while trusting God's freedom, so that we neither presume upon deliverance nor doubt God's goodness when it does not come.

debates.question: What does the church mean by 'It must be his angel,' verse 15?

views.label: A guardian angel assigned to Peter
views.case: Many take it as a popular belief that each person has an angel who can take on the person's appearance or voice. Jesus' words about the little ones whose angels always see the face of the Father, Matthew 18:10, are often offered as background. On this view the believers assume that Peter must have died and that his angel has come to announce it.

views.label: A messenger or Peter's spirit after death
views.case: Others take the word to mean a messenger from Peter, or his spirit. The Greek can mean either a heavenly being or a human envoy. Hebrews 1:14 describes angels as sent to serve those who will inherit salvation, which fits a general picture of angels serving, but not a specific guardian per person.

debates.bearing: Luke does not endorse or correct the belief. He reports it as an honest guess by astonished people, and the point is that they were wrong and the answer to their prayer was standing at the door.

debates.question: Is Luke's account of Herod's death compatible with Josephus?

views.label: Yes, they describe the same event from different angles
views.case: Both place the scene at Caesarea, with royal robes, a crowd calling the king a god, and sudden fatal illness. Josephus tells of a pain in the stomach, Luke of worms, and the two can describe one condition in clinical and moral terms. Luke's focus is theological, on why it happened, where Josephus is concerned with the omen.

views.label: They reflect different traditions and cannot be fully reconciled
views.case: Some historians note differences in setting, in the length of the illness, and in the cause, and conclude that Luke and Josephus drew on separate accounts. On this reading Luke's value is in the interpretation more than the medical detail.

debates.bearing: The agreement on the central facts, a public acclamation as a god followed by sudden death, is strong evidence that Luke reports a known event, while the differences warn us not to demand that two ancient writers record the same details.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the prayer in verse 5. Luke uses an adverb, ektenos, 'fervently', and a construction that stresses duration: prayer 'was being made' by the church. The word describes something stretched out, strained like a muscle. The same root marks the way Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, more earnestly, Luke 22:44, and the way Peter later tells believers to love one another deeply, 1 Peter 4:8. The church's prayer is not a quick request but a sustained pull on God.

Next is the guard. Luke says four tetradia, groups of four, which shows the soldiers were arranged in the Roman manner. The word for what Peter does, sleeping between two soldiers, uses a participle that shows a continued state, and the angel has to strike him, patasso, on the side to wake him. The verb is strong; it is used for striking with a sword, as in Acts 12:23, where the angel 'struck' Herod down. The same angel uses the same verb on Peter and Herod, a nudge for one and a death blow for the other.

The gate opens automate, 'by itself'. This is the root of our word automatic, and in the New Testament it appears only here and in Mark 4:28, where the earth bears grain of itself. In both cases the idea is that something happens without human hand. Luke is making the point that the door opens not by trickery or bribery but by God's power.

Peter, in verse 11, says the Lord 'rescued' him. The verb exaireo, to take out, to deliver, is used in the Old Testament and in Acts for God's rescue of Joseph from his troubles, Acts 7:10, and of Israel in the exodus, Acts 7:34, where God says He has come down to deliver them. Peter's use of it puts his night in the line of those deliverances. It also fits his words that he was rescued from Herod's hand, a Greek phrase of 'hand' that matches Herod's own act in verse 1, where he put forth hands to harm the church.

The maid's name is Rhoda, which means 'rose', and Luke says she 'recognised' Peter's voice, epignousa. She is identified by voice and not by sight, and her joy is such that she forgets to open the gate. A nice detail: the word for the gate, pylon, is also the word for a gateway or porch of a house.

Finally, in verse 23 Herod is eaten by worms, skolekobrotos. The word is rare and unpleasant, and it paints a death that is slow and humiliating. Luke's verdict is introduced with the Greek 'because', anth' hon, giving the reason: he did not give the glory to God. The word doxa, glory, is exactly the word that Isaiah 42:8 says God will not yield to another.

typology.type: Peter's night as a second Passover, Exodus 12:11
typology.fulfillment: At Passover Israel ate dressed for travel, sandals on the feet, staff in hand, while the angel of judgment passed through Egypt, Exodus 12:11 to 12. Peter is told to dress, put on sandals, wrap his cloak and follow. The exodus pattern of a night rescue, with the tyrant judged and the people led out, is repeated in miniature. In Christ the pattern reaches its centre, since His own death falls at Passover and He leads His people out of bondage to sin, 1 Corinthians 5:7. The correspondence is a family likeness, not a one to one prediction, and it falls short because Peter was freed from one prison for a time, whereas Christ frees from death itself.

typology.type: The king who takes God's glory, Ezekiel 28 and Daniel 4
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel told the ruler of Tyre that he had said 'I am a god' though he was a man, Ezekiel 28:2, and Nebuchadnezzar was struck while boasting of his own majesty, Daniel 4:30 to 31. Herod, hailed as a god by crowds from Tyre and Sidon, repeats the pattern of the proud ruler brought low. The pattern finds its last form in the man of lawlessness who takes his seat in God's temple, 2 Thessalonians 2:4, and in the beast that blasphemes, Revelation 13. Herod falls short of that final figure because his claim is made by flatterers, not by himself, and his end comes at once.

James and his brother John once asked for places of honour, and Jesus answered, 'You will drink the cup that I drink, and you will be baptized with the baptism that I undergo,' Mark 10:39. James is the first of the Twelve to do it, killed by the sword in Acts 12:2. His death fits the pattern of the follower walking the road of the Master, and Paul can later say that he is completing in his flesh what is lacking in Christ's afflictions, Colossians 1:24. The pattern is not a reenactment of the cross, for no martyr's death atones for sin. It points to a life of sharing in His sufferings, as Peter himself would, John 21:18 to 19.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ first by contrast with the king. Herod Agrippa sat on a throne in robes that shone, and a crowd shouted that he was a god. The true King had been robed in mockery and enthroned on a cross. Herod's reign depended on pleasing the crowd, as Pilate had also wished to satisfy the crowd, Mark 15:15, but Jesus is the King whose authority rests on the Father's will. Herod gives no glory to God and dies at once; Jesus prayed, 'yet not My will, but Yours be done,' Luke 22:42, and was raised. The chapter lets us see two kinds of kingship, one that takes glory and one that gives it.

It points to Christ by the pattern of Passover. Peter is led out at the feast of Unleavened Bread, a Passover night, dressed and sandalled, while the king who meant to execute him is outwitted. The exodus is the Old Testament's great rescue, and its New Testament fulfilment is the Lamb. Paul says, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. The angel at Peter's cell recalls the exodus, but the freeing that matters most is the one Christ accomplished, in which the prison is death and the keys are His, Revelation 1:18.

The chapter points to Christ by promise. In Matthew 16:18 He told this very man that He would build His church and the gates of Hades would not prevail against it. In Acts 12 the gates are not only of Hades but of iron, and in neither case do they stand. Jesus had also told Peter how he would die, John 21:18 to 19. The rescue is therefore not an escape from Christ's word but a delay within it. Peter is not saved from death, only for a time, so that his death in its season will glorify God.

It points to Christ by the prayer. The church prays to the Father about Peter, and the answer comes through an angel of the Lord. The believers who are praying are the same ones who in Acts 4:24 to 28 prayed in the light of Psalm 2, remembering that Herod and Pilate gathered against God's holy servant Jesus. In both cases the rulers gather, and in both the Lord laughs at them, Psalm 2:4.

Be careful with the details. The sleeping Peter is not a picture of Christ in the tomb, and the angel is not Christ, even though Christ is the Lord who sends angels. The links above are the ones the text and the New Testament make: a king set against a King, a Passover set against the Lamb, and a church that is being built and cannot be stopped.
study.god:
The chapter's firmest claim about God is that He is not outmatched. The chapter piles up human power: a king, a soldier's guard of sixteen, chains, a locked gate, and a city eager for a spectacle. Against this Luke places a sleeping man and a praying room. God does not engage by matching force with force. He sends one angel, who walks through the entire system without anyone noticing, and the gate opens by itself. The point is not that God is stronger by degrees but that human security is no obstacle to Him at all.

He is free. Luke does not allow us to turn God into a mechanism. James dies, Peter lives. God rescues Peter while the guards, who had no part in the escape, are put to death by Herod, verse 19. Nothing in the chapter explains why, and the silence is itself a lesson. The God of the Bible is not required to explain Himself, and He is not forced by the intensity of our prayers. Yet He is not arbitrary: the same chapter ends with the word of God multiplying, which shows His purposes are steady even when His methods are not.

He hears prayer. The church prays 'fervently', and Luke carefully reports that the answer happens as they pray. The God of the whole earth is attentive to a room of frightened believers, and He answers beyond what they dared to ask for, since they were not expecting Peter at the door. This is the God who invites us to ask because He delights in giving.

He is jealous for His glory, and just in guarding it. Isaiah 42:8 says He will not yield His glory to another, and Herod's death is the plain sequel. The reason Luke gives is not cruelty or pride in the king, but that he did not give glory to God. God shares many things with His creatures, including His image, His Spirit and His kingdom, but not His worship. The line is drawn in the book of Acts, as in Acts 10:26 when Peter lifts Cornelius from his knees and says he is only a man, and in Acts 14:15.

He is the Lord who reigns through ordinary means. Peter's rescue comes with an angel, but the church's role is a prayer meeting, and Luke's narrative closes with a mundane note, Barnabas and Saul returning with John Mark. The grandeur of God and the smallness of His instruments are held together.

For worship, the chapter invites trust that does not need to be proved by outcomes. Peter could sleep because the Lord sustains him, as the psalmist says, 'I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me,' Psalm 3:5. To worship such a God is to pray with persistence, to give Him the glory in all things, and to hold loosely both rescue and loss, as Paul would in prison, 2 Timothy 4:17 to 18.

crossReferences.note: The first Passover was eaten in haste, dressed for travel, sandals on, while God struck the gods of Egypt. Peter is told to dress, put on sandals and follow on a Passover night while a king who tried to hold God's people is judged. The echo marks his rescue as a small exodus.

An earlier jailbreak. An angel of the Lord opened the doors for the apostles and told them to go and speak in the temple. The two escapes are told alike, but in chapter 5 the apostles return to preach publicly while in chapter 12 Peter leaves for another place. Luke shows the same God working in different ways.

The church prayed with one voice using Psalm 2, remembering that Herod and Pilate gathered against Jesus. Acts 12 shows the next Herod meeting the fate the psalm predicts for rulers who rage against the Lord and His Anointed One.

The nations rage and the kings take their stand against the Lord, but the One enthroned in heaven laughs. This is the pattern of chapter 12, in which the plotting king is mocked by events, for his guards cannot hold a man and his throne cannot hold him.

Nebuchadnezzar was struck at the moment he boasted of the glory of his majesty, and later praised the King of heaven. Herod is struck as the crowd cries that he is a god. The pattern teaches that God humbles those who take glory, though only Nebuchadnezzar is restored.

The ruler of Tyre claimed to be a god though he was a man. Herod's crowd came from Tyre and Sidon, and the same boast is made for him. The old oracle shows that the divine verdict on such claims is fixed.

God says He will not yield His glory to another. This is the principle behind Luke's reason in Acts 12:23, that Herod did not give glory to God. Luke applies it to a historical event with the bluntness of a prophet.

James and John asked for the seats of honour and Jesus said they would drink His cup. James becomes the first apostle to do so, in Acts 12:2. The promise had been plain from the start, and the cup was not a surprise.

Jesus told Peter he would one day stretch out his hands and be led where he did not want to go, indicating the death by which he would glorify God. This helps explain why Peter was rescued in Acts 12 only for a time, since his end was already known and fixed.

Jesus promised that He would build His church and that the gates of Hades would not prevail against it. In Acts 12 an iron gate and a king's design both fail. The chapter is a concrete instance of the promise to the man who first heard it.

The Israelites were fruitful and multiplied in Egypt even under a king who tried to crush them. The phrase 'spread and multiply' in Acts 12:24 echoes that language, and so places the church under Herod in the line of Israel under Pharaoh.

The first of three growth reports using the verbs for increase and multiplication. Here they follow the persecution of Stephen; in 12:24 they follow the death of James and the judgment on Herod; in 19:20 they follow the defeat of the sorcerers. Each shows opposition failing to stop the word.

The author urges believers to remember those in prison as if they were bound with them. The praying church of Acts 12 is a living example, and the note of fervency in verse 5 shows what that remembering looks like when a leader is held by the state.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a blessing, 'Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth,' Genesis 1:28, and almost at once the story is about a conflict over that blessing. The serpent tries to unmake it, Cain kills his brother, Pharaoh tries to drown Israel's sons, and in the New Testament Herod the Great tries to kill the infant Jesus. Each time the question is the same: can a power in the world stop what God has said? Acts 12 gives the church's answer in a single sentence, that the word of God continued to spread and multiply.

That sentence is the language of creation and of the exodus placed in the mouth of the church. In Egypt the Israelites were fruitful and multiplied under a king who tried to cut them off. Now under another king the new Israel does the same. The Passover night, the angel, the open way and the judged tyrant are all there. The chapter shows that the Lord who redeemed Israel is the Lord who stands behind the church, and that His ancient pattern of rescue and judgment has not been retired.

It also continues the story of the Herods. The first Herod sought the child's life; the second, Antipas, mocked Him; the third, Agrippa, killed His apostle and was himself brought down. The last of them, Agrippa II, will listen to Paul and say he is almost persuaded, Acts 26:28. Their family is the story of earthly power meeting the gospel, and every time the gospel outlives them.

Acts 12 also teaches what the Bible's later chapters will confirm, that the cost of following Jesus is real. James is killed, and Peter is delivered for a time, and Paul will end in a Roman prison, writing that the time of his departure is at hand, 2 Timothy 4:6. Rescue and martyrdom both belong to the story, and neither is a defeat.

The new creation will end the contest. The one who holds the keys of Death and Hades, Revelation 1:18, will bring all prisons to an end. Rulers who claim divinity will be brought low, and the multitude of the redeemed will give the glory to God, who alone is worthy. In that city the doors are never shut, Revelation 21:25, and no angel has to tap a sleeper on the side to lead him out, for the people of God will live in the light of His presence for ever.

quiz.q: What did the church do while Peter was in prison?

options.text: It prayed fervently to God for him.
options.note: Verse 5 says the church was earnestly praying to God for Peter, the pivot of the whole rescue.

options.text: It gathered anxiously at Mary's house, uncertain whether God would act.
options.note: True to the scene, they did gather and were slow to believe, but Luke's stress falls on their fervent prayer, not their doubt.

options.text: It organized a plan to break Peter out by force.
options.note: There is no armed rescue here; the church's only weapon was prayer, and God sent the angel.

options.text: It kept quiet and did nothing, fearing Herod.
options.note: Far from doing nothing, the church prayed fervently through the night.

quiz.q: How did Peter get out of the prison?

options.text: An angel of the Lord woke him, loosed his chains, and led him past the guards and the iron gate.
options.note: Verses 7 to 10 describe the angel freeing Peter as gates opened by themselves.

options.text: God delivered him through supernatural means while he slept between the soldiers.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it leaves out the specific agent, the angel of the Lord who led him out.

options.text: The guards fell asleep and Peter slipped away on his own.
options.note: The guards were still in place; the deliverance was the angel's doing, not Peter's stealth.

options.text: Herod relented and released him.
options.note: Herod intended to execute Peter and later ordered the guards punished; he did not release him.

options.text: Because he accepted the crowd's praise as a god and did not give glory to God.
options.note: Verse 23 states he was struck because he did not give God the glory.

options.text: Because he had killed James and imprisoned Peter.
options.note: His persecution was real wickedness, but Luke names the immediate cause as his stealing God's glory.

options.text: Because he mismanaged the dispute with Tyre and Sidon.
options.note: That dispute sets the scene, but it was not the reason for the judgment.

options.text: Because he was old and simply fell ill.
options.note: Luke attributes his death directly to God's judgment, not natural causes alone.

quiz.q: What is the point of the chapter's final verse?

options.text: The word of God kept spreading and multiplying despite the king's opposition.
options.note: Verse 24 crowns the chapter: the true King's word is unstoppable.

options.text: Barnabas and Saul returned to Antioch with John Mark.
options.note: That happens in verse 25 and sets up the mission, but the theological climax is the advancing word in verse 24.

options.text: The church finally felt safe from persecution.
options.note: The chapter does not promise safety; it promises the word's advance amid ongoing danger.

options.text: The gospel had reached its limit in Jerusalem.
options.note: The opposite is true: the word keeps multiplying and is about to go to the nations.

quiz.q: How does this chapter contrast the two kings?

options.text: Herod grasps glory and is judged, while the ascended Christ rescues His servant and reigns over all.
options.note: The whole chapter sets the dying, glory-grasping king against the living Lord whose word cannot be chained.

options.text: Herod is powerful on earth, but God is powerful in heaven.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it misses the sharp reversal by which the earthly king falls and the heavenly King prevails.

options.text: Both kings are shown to rule justly in their own spheres.
options.note: Herod does not rule justly; he persecutes the church and steals God's glory.

options.text: The chapter treats Herod as the rightful ruler God endorses.
options.note: God strikes Herod down; he is the false king set against the true.

questions: The church could not fight Herod, so it prayed. When you feel powerless against forces bigger than you, does prayer feel like your first resort or your last? What would change if it were your first?
God rescued Peter but did not spare James. How do you hold on to God's goodness when He delivers one person and not another?
The praying believers could hardly believe Peter was really at the door. Where have you prayed for something and then been surprised, even doubtful, when God answered?
Herod fell because he took glory that belonged to God. Where are you tempted to take credit or applause that you should be handing back to God?
The word of God kept spreading no matter what Herod did. How does the unstoppable advance of the gospel steady you when the church seems weak or under pressure today?

translationNotes.note: King Herod here is Herod Agrippa the First; the BSB footnote makes this explicit. The phrase rendered reached out to harm is literally put forth the hands to mistreat.
The Feast of Unleavened Bread and the Passover, mentioned in verses 3 and 4, set Peter's rescue against the backdrop of Israel's exodus deliverance, a link Luke's readers would feel.

Manuscripts differ over whether Barnabas and Saul returned to Jerusalem or from Jerusalem; the BSB reads returned to Jerusalem, with the alternate from Jerusalem noted. The sense of the mission being fulfilled is the same.
